# 2 Kings 25 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

The chapter records the final collapse of Jerusalem (586 BC): the 18-month siege, the capture and blinding of Zedekiah, the burning of the temple and palace, the breaking down of the walls, the third deportation, the brief governorship and assassination of Gedaliah, the flight to Egypt, and finally the release of Jehoiachin from prison in Babylon — a faint but real glimmer of hope that God had not abandoned the line of David.

---

## v. 1 — The Siege Begins

- **Precision of the date.** This is the most specific date in all of Kings (year, month, and day). The exactness is corroborated by Jeremiah 39:2, Jeremiah 52:4, and Ezekiel 24:1. Such precision indicates the extreme importance of the event. The date corresponds to December/January 588 BC and later became a day of fasting and remembrance for Israel (cf. Zech 8:19). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-25-commentary)

- **Nebuchadnezzar as God's instrument.** Scripture elsewhere calls Nebuchadnezzar "My servant" (Jeremiah 25:9). He was the human agent, but the siege was ultimately God's judgment. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-25-commentary)

- **The siege wall (Hebrew *dāyēq*).** This was not a quick frontal assault but a methodical encirclement — siege ramparts, watchtowers, and movable towers designed to starve the population into surrender. The Babylonians "relied initially on tight control using 'watch towers' rather than siege works, allowing those who wished to leave to do so." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-25/)

- **First time a foreign era is used.** "This is the first time in Kings that an event in the history of Israel is dated by a foreign era" (Dilday), marking the loss of national autonomy. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-25/)

- **Not a direct march.** According to the Pulpit Commentary, Nebuchadnezzar's army first spread over Judea, capturing fortified towns like Lachish and Azekah to cut off Zedekiah's line of communication with Egypt, before investing Jerusalem itself. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-25-commentary)

---

## v. 2 — The Length of the Siege

- **Eighteen months.** The siege lasted from the ninth year, tenth month to the eleventh year, fourth month — about one year, five months, and twenty-seven days. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-25.html, via search excerpt)

- **Brief interruption.** Jeremiah 37:5 and Ezekiel 17:17 record that Pharaoh Hophra (Apries) of Egypt marched to relieve Jerusalem. Nebuchadnezzar temporarily lifted the siege to meet him. The Egyptians retired without a decisive battle, and the siege resumed. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-25-commentary)

- **Inexorable divine judgment.** The prolonged duration emphasised that judgment was inescapable and complete — "the city endured an inescapable judgment that unfolded exactly as God had spoken." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-25-commentary)

---

## v. 3 — Famine

- **The siege achieved its goal.** The famine became so severe that "there was no food for the people of the land." The Hebrew word *ra'ab* conveys extreme scarcity leading to starvation. Bob Utley notes that "the people of the land" in this period referred to the landed aristocracy, not the poor. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-25-commentary)

- **Covenant curses fulfilled.** The horrors of this famine — including cannibalism, with mothers eating their own children (Lamentations 2:20; 4:10) — fulfilled the covenant curses of Deuteronomy 28:53–57, which had warned of precisely such horrors if Israel was unfaithful. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-25-commentary)

- **Famine followed by pestilence.** Pulpit Commentary notes that as often happens in sieges, famine was followed by pestilence (Jeremiah 21:6–7). Ezekiel 5:12 says a third of the inhabitants died of famine and plague. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-25-commentary)

- **Even Jeremiah nearly starved.** Jeremiah 38:9 records that the prophet, cast into a cistern, was at risk of dying "because of the famine, for there is no more bread in the city." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-25-commentary)

---

## v. 4 — The City Breached; Zedekiah Flees

- **The breach.** The Chaldeans broke through the northern wall of the city. Ellicott notes this was the Lower City; after entering, the Babylonian generals proceeded to "the middle gate" — the gate in the north wall of Zion separating the upper from the lower city (Jeremiah 39:3). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-25.html, via search excerpt)

- **Flight by night.** The king and his men of war fled under cover of darkness "by way of the gate between the two walls near the king's garden," heading toward the Arabah (the Jordan Valley). MacLaren observes, "Down the rocky road went the flying host … The king's flight by night had been foretold by Ezekiel far away in captivity (Ezekiel 12:12)." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mac/2-kings-25.html, via search excerpt)

- **Emotional restraint of the narrative.** MacLaren remarks, "The passionless tone of the narrative here is very remarkable. Not a word escapes the writer to show his feelings, though he is telling his country's fall … It is all one long sentence, for in the Hebrew each verse begins with 'and,' clause heaped on clause, as if each were a footstep of the destroying angel in his slow, irresistible march." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mac/2-kings-25.html, via search excerpt)

- **The Hebrew text is defective** at this point, lacking a verb and mention of the king; the parallels in Jeremiah 39:4 and 52:7 supply the missing material: "And Zedekiah king of Judah and all the men of war fled." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-25.html, via search excerpt)

---

## v. 5 — Capture in the Plains of Jericho

- **A deeply ironic location.** Zedekiah was captured in the plains of Jericho — the very spot where Israel first entered the Promised Land under Joshua. "Here, where Israel experienced her first victory as the walls of Jericho fell before unarmed men who trusted God, was the scene of her last defeat." (Dilday, quoted in Enduring Word). MacLaren adds: "The end came back to the beginning, and the cradle was the coffin." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-25/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mac/2-kings-25.html, via search excerpt)

- **Deserted by his army.** "All his army was separated from him" — his whole army scattered, leaving the king alone to face capture. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-25/)

---

## v. 6 — Brought to Riblah for Judgment

- **Riblah** was Nebuchadnezzar's military headquarters in the land of Hamath (modern Syria). Zedekiah was brought there for judgment rather than to Babylon itself. The singular verbs in Jeremiah's parallel account (Jer 39:6; 52:10–11) attribute the acts directly to Nebuchadnezzar, though he may have acted through agents. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-25.html, via search excerpt)

---

## v. 7 — The Blinding of Zedekiah

- **Sons slaughtered before his eyes.** The Babylonians made certain that the last sight Zedekiah ever saw was the murder of his own sons. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-25/)

- **Fulfilment of Ezekiel 12:13.** God had promised through Ezekiel: "I will bring him to Babylon, to the land of the Chaldeans; yet he shall not see it, though he shall die there." This seeming contradiction was fulfilled exactly: Zedekiah saw the king of Babylon at Riblah (fulfilling Jeremiah 32:5; 34:3), was then blinded, and was taken to Babylon where he died without ever seeing it. F.B. Meyer notes that "two prophecies which appeared to be contradictory were reconciled and fulfilled." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-25/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/fbm/2-kings-25.html, via search excerpt)

- **Babylonian practice.** Blinding was a known Babylonian punishment (Herodotus 7.18). Assyrian sculptures depict kings blinding captives. Zedekiah was then bound with bronze (literally "double brass") shackles — manacles and fetters. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-25.html, via search excerpt)

- **Keil & Delitzsch:** The punishment was "the merited reward of the breach of his oath" to Nebuchadnezzar and his "hardening himself against the counsel of the Lord" announced by Jeremiah — that he could have saved Jerusalem by voluntary surrender (Jeremiah 38:17ff). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/2-kings-25.html, via search excerpt)

- **Trapp's spiritual observation:** "The eyes of whose mind had been put out long before; else he might have foreseen and prevented this evil." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-25/)

- **Josephus** (*Antiquities* 10.8.8) says Nebuchadnezzar "kept Zedekiah in prison until he died; and then buried him magnificently," agreeing with Jeremiah 34:5. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-25/)

---

## vv. 8–10 — The Destruction of Jerusalem

- **v. 8: Nebuzaradan enters.** On the seventh day of the fifth month, in the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar (586 BC), Nebuzaradan — "captain of the guard," literally "chief executioner" or "the slaughterer" — entered Jerusalem. This was about a month after the city wall was breached. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-25/)

- **v. 9: The temple burned.** Solomon's temple, which had stood for over 400 years (Clarke calculates 424 years, 3 months, and 8 days from its foundation), was burned to the ground along with the royal palace and every significant house. The Talmud declares the Babylonians held a two-day feast inside the temple to desecrate it before setting fire on the third day. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-25/)

- **Constable: theological significance.** "His burning of Yahweh's house was a statement that the Babylonians had overcome Yahweh as much as it was an effort to keep the remaining Judahites from worshipping Him. In the ancient Near East, the condition of the house (temple) of a god reflected on that god's reputation." This would have thoroughly demoralised even the godly. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-25.html)

- **v. 10: Walls broken down.** The breaking down of Jerusalem's walls "prevented the inhabitants from defending themselves but also visualized the fact that Judah no longer had any defense. Yahweh had been her defense." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-25.html)

- **F.B. Meyer** suggests that a few years later, Nebuchadnezzar's golden image on the plains of Dura (Daniel 3:1) may have been made from the metal removed from the Holy City. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/fbm/2-kings-25.html, via search excerpt)

---

## vv. 11–12 — The Third Deportation

- **v. 11: Remaining people exiled.** Nebuzaradan carried away the rest of the population, including those who had defected to the Babylonians during the siege. This was the third major deportation. Only Jeremiah and Gedaliah were left behind of the prominent men (Jeremiah 39:11–14). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-25/)

- **v. 12: The poorest left.** Only "the poorest of the land" were left to tend the vineyards and fields. This ensured the land would not go entirely to waste but also prevented any organised resistance — those left had neither wealth nor influence. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-25/)

---

## vv. 13–17 — The Plundering of the Temple

- **v. 13: Bronze articles broken up.** The Chaldeans broke into pieces the bronze pillars, the movable stands, and the bronze Sea. The bronze was carried to Babylon. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-25/)

- **v. 14–15: All temple utensils taken.** Pots, shovels, wick trimmers, dishes, censers, sprinkling bowls — everything of bronze, gold, or silver used in temple service was removed. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-25/)

- **v. 16: Bronze beyond measure.** The weight of bronze from the two pillars, the Sea, and the stands was so great it could not be calculated. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-25/)

- **v. 17: The pillars described.** Each pillar was 18 cubits (about 27 feet) tall; the bronze capital was 3 cubits high, with a network of pomegranates. Constable notes the theological significance of the pillars' names: **Jachin** ("He establishes") and **Boaz** ("in Him is strength"). "Israel, which God had established (Jachin), had suffered destruction. Israel's strength (Boaz) had also departed from her because of her apostasy." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-25.html)

- **The Ark of the Covenant.** Constable adds: "Most scholars believe the Babylonians either destroyed the ark of the covenant or took it to Babylon from which it never returned to Jerusalem … A few believe the Jews hid it under the temple esplanade." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-25.html)

---

## vv. 18–21 — Execution of Leaders at Riblah

- **v. 18: Religious leaders seized.** Seraiah the chief priest (grandson of Hilkiah who found the Book of the Law under Josiah), Zephaniah the second priest, and the three doorkeepers were taken. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-25/)

- **v. 19: Civil and military leaders.** A court official over the men of war, five royal advisors, the scribe of the army captain who enlisted the people, and sixty men of the land were taken. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-25/)

- **v. 20–21: Executed at Riblah.** Nebuchadnezzar struck them down at Riblah in the land of Hamath. Constable explains the theological significance: "The Babylonians also cut the priesthood back so the people could not unite around it and rebel. Its temporary termination also meant that Israel was no longer able to worship God as He had prescribed … Access to God as the Mosaic Law specified was no longer possible." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-25.html)

- **"Judah was taken into exile, away from its own land."** This was the land God gave His people. They had possessed it for some 860 years; they took it by faith and obedience but lost it through idolatry and sin. Clarke calculates 468 years from David's reign, 388 years from the division of the kingdoms, and 134 years from the fall of Israel. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-25/)

---

## vv. 22–24 — Gedaliah Appointed Governor

- **v. 22: Gedaliah son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan.** Gedaliah came from a godly family — his father Ahikam had protected Jeremiah (Jeremiah 26:24), and his grandfather Shaphan had been Josiah's scribe who read the Book of the Law. He was a friend of Jeremiah (Jeremiah 39:14) and, like his father, had advised surrender to Babylon. Josephus describes him as "gentle and generous." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-25/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jgc/2-kings-25.html, via search excerpt)

- **v. 23: Commanders come to Mizpah.** Ishmael (of royal blood), Johanan, Seraiah, and Jaazaniah — commanders who had escaped the Babylonians — came to Gedaliah at Mizpah (about 8 miles north of Jerusalem). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-25/)

- **v. 24: Gedaliah's oath.** He swore to them, "Do not be afraid … Live in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it will be well with you." Enduring Word notes: "It seemed unpatriotic and perhaps ungodly to do this, but it was the right thing to do … In this situation, to resist the Babylonians was to resist God." This was the same counsel Jeremiah had given all along. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-25/)

---

## vv. 25–26 — Assassination of Gedaliah; Flight to Egypt

- **v. 25: Ishmael's treachery.** Ishmael, of royal lineage, came with ten men and assassinated Gedaliah, along with the Judeans and Chaldeans at Mizpah. The full account in Jeremiah 40–41 reveals that Ishmael was acting at the instigation of the king of Ammon, and that Gedaliah had been warned by Johanan but refused to believe the threat. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-25/)

- **Reformed perspective (Ligonier):** "Ishmael the son of Nethaniah had royal pedigree, and no doubt some of the Judahites left behind hoped he would restore their independence by killing Gedaliah, the Babylonian-appointed governor. But … the point is clear: Judah was not to look for hope in the overthrow of Babylon." The assassination was an attempt at violent restoration that was "ill conceived" (cf. Jeremiah 42–43). (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/glimmer-of-hope-for-judah)

- **v. 26: Flight to Egypt.** All the people, "small and great," together with the army commanders, fled to Egypt for fear of Chaldean reprisals. They took Jeremiah with them against his counsel (Jeremiah 42–44). "In this case, going to Egypt was worse than submitting to the judgment of God brought through the Babylonians." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-25/)

- **Historical note.** Dilday observes: "The existence of the Jews in Egypt in the fifth century is now illustrated by the Elephantine Papyri." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-25/)

---

## vv. 27–30 — Jehoiachin Released in Babylon

- **v. 27: The date.** The twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month of the thirty-seventh year of Jehoiachin's captivity (561 BC). Evil-merodach (Amel-Marduk), son and successor of Nebuchadnezzar, released Jehoiachin from prison in the year he began to reign. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-25/)

- **A deliberate ending.** The author could have ended at v. 21 with the destruction of Jerusalem. Why include vv. 27–30? Because the original audience was the exiles in Babylon, and this appendix answers their question: "Now that we know why God sent us to Babylon, where is our hope for the future?" (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/glimmer-of-hope-for-judah)

- **v. 28: Kindness and honour.** Evil-merodach spoke kindly to Jehoiachin and set his throne above the thrones of other captive kings in Babylon. "This resulted from an agreement (*mt*, 'spoke good things with him') rather than just generally spoke kindly to him" (Wiseman). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-25/)

- **v. 29: Changed garments and the king's table.** Jehoiachin changed out of his prison clothes and dined regularly at the king's table — a mark of honour and provision. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-25/)

- **v. 30: A daily portion.** The king provided a regular daily allowance for the rest of his life — "a day's portion in its day." Ellicott comments: "The writer evidently dwells with pleasure on this faint gleam of light amid the darkness of the exile. It was a kind of foreshadowing of the pity which afterwards was to be extended to the captive people." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-25.html, via search excerpt)

- **Reformed perspective (Ligonier):** "His exaltation in Babylon over all the other captive kings was a faint glimmer of hope that God's people yet had a future. David's line would continue somehow through Jehoiachin. In fact, it would be more accurate to say that the people were to put their hope not in Jehoiachin but in the promise-keeping Lord who covenanted to preserve David's throne forever. David's line was chastened but not abandoned." (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/glimmer-of-hope-for-judah)

- **Charismatic/Pentecostal perspective (Enduring Word):** "The final words of the Book of 2 Kings describe small kindnesses and blessings given in the worst circumstances … looking for even small notes of grace and mercy as evidences of the returning favor of God … This was small, but evidence nonetheless that God was not done blessing and restoring His people, foreshadowing even greater blessing and restoration to come." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-25/)

- **Wiseman:** "This second appendix is added to remind the reader that while Jehoiachin was still in Babylon as the representative of David's dynasty God still preserved his people. Some see this as intended to end the history on a hopeful note, perhaps even of 'Messianic revival'." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-25/)

- **Keil (via Coffman):** "This event was intended as a comforting sign to the whole of the captive people, that the Lord would one day put an end to their banishment, if they would acknowledge that their captivity was a well-deserved punishment for their sins." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/2-kings-25.html, via search excerpt)

- **F.B. Meyer's application:** "Is it to be supposed that the king of Babylon took more care of Jehoiachin than God will take care of us?" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-25/)

- **Jewish tradition (Trapp):** "The Rabbins tell us that, his father returning to his right mind, after that he had for seven years' space been turned a-grazing among the beasts of the field, cast Evil-merodach into the same prison with Jehoiachin, who told him his case, and thereby found this favour with him." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-25/)

---

## Points of Traditional Distinctiveness

- **Reformed (Ligonier):** The emphasis falls on God's sovereign faithfulness to His covenant. The release of Jehoiachin is not primarily about Jehoiachin himself but about the promise-keeping God who preserves David's line. The assassination of Gedaliah teaches that hope must not be placed in violent political overthrow but in God's promises. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/glimmer-of-hope-for-judah)

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** The emphasis is pastoral and applicational — God's mercy shines even in darkest judgment; believers should accept discipline humbly and do right in their circumstances rather than resist or run. The final four verses are read as "small notes of grace and mercy" that foreshadow restoration. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-25/)

- **Evangelical (Precept Austin / Constable):** Strong emphasis on in-depth exegesis, Hebrew word studies (*dāyēq*, *ra'ab*), historical and archaeological corroboration, and how the events fulfil specific covenant curses. Constable draws theological meaning from the temple pillars' names and the cutting off of the priesthood. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-25-commentary ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-25.html)
